verses.translation_literal: Not to us, YHWH, not to us, [but] to your name give glory, on your covenant loyalty, on your faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Not to us, LORD. Not to us. We will not have it said that the glory is ours. Give it to your name, and let it rest on your steadfast love, on your faithfulness that does not fail.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a double refusal, and the actors should play it as two beats, not one: the first 'not to us' is a breath, the second is a vow. Radak says the repetition is to strengthen the point. This is the voice of a people who know they have no claim, asking for rescue on another ground altogether: God's own name, his reputation among the nations. Rashi hears it as 'not on account of us and the quality of our deeds'; Metzudat David as 'not for the sake of our righteousness'.

The KJV's 'for thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake' is serviceable, but 'mercy' is soft for chesed, the loyalty that flows from covenant, and 'truth' for emet misses its sense of dependability: this is the God whose word holds. The two Hebrew phrases are bare, 'al chasdekha 'al amitekha, with 'al meaning 'on the ground of' or, as Radak glosses, 'concerning'. Note too that 'give glory' is an imperative addressed to God: the people tell God what to do with his own honour. In the ancient Near East a god's name was his standing; a defeated people meant a diminished deity.

philological_notes.note: 'to your name': the name stands for God's reputation and presence in the world. The petition rests on what happens to that name if Israel is shamed, which v.2 spells out.
Covenant loyalty, the faithfulness that a stronger party owes by its own pledge; paired with emet, 'reliability', it names the two grounds on which God is asked to act.

verses.translation_literal: Why will the nations say, "Where, please, [is] their God?"
verses.translation_dramatic: Why should the nations say it? Why should they stand over us and sneer, "Where is he now, this God of theirs?"
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the reason behind the prayer: the taunt. The mocking question is a cry of triumph from the victors, and Radak hears in it the assumption that if God had power he would rise and help. Meiri adds that the nations scorn a God they cannot see. The Hebrew nagging 'na' is a small word of insistence or sarcasm; 'where, pray, is...' (YLT) keeps the sneer, while the KJV's 'Wherefore should the heathen say' turns goyim into 'heathen', a loaded English word that the Hebrew does not carry: it simply says 'nations'.

Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion gloss 'na' as 'now', which is how KJV and ASV rendered it ('Where is now their God?'). In the ancient world a god who did not defend his people was proved weak; the question is a theological verdict as well as an insult. The same taunt appears in Joel 2:17 and Psalm 79:10.

philological_notes.note: 'Where, please / where now?': na is a particle of urgency, here mocking. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as 'now'.

verses.translation_literal: And our God [is] in the heavens; all that he desired he did.
verses.translation_dramatic: But our God is in the heavens, and he is not idle there. Whatever he has wished, he has done.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer comes quietly, with a confident 'and', almost an aside: the nations ask where God is, and the singers tell them. He is in the heavens. This is no retreat. Radak says the nations do not know the difference between our God and theirs: ours rules above and below and does what he wills; theirs does not. Malbim reads it as an answer to the notion that God has withdrawn his presence to the heavens: even from there, 'all that he desired he did'.

The perfect tense 'asah, 'he did', states a settled fact, not a hope; the KJV's 'hath done whatsoever he hath pleased' carries that well. The point is a contrast already forming: the God who acts at will in heaven against idols made by hands on earth. Note that chafetz, 'delighted in, desired', is the language of free will, not of need.

philological_notes.note: 'to delight in, desire': God's sovereign will. The perfect here is a statement of fact rather than a past event: whatever he has wished, he has accomplished.

verses.translation_literal: Their idols [are] silver and gold, the work of the hands of humankind.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their idols? Silver and gold. The work of hands, of human hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer turns on the nations' gods. The sting lies in the contrast with v.3: our God does what he wills in the heavens, their gods are made by human hands. The word for 'idols' is 'atzabbim, which sounds like 'etzev, 'pain, grief': Ibn Ezra and Radak both explain that these are called 'sorrows' because they bring grief to those who trust them, and Meiri adds that those who trust them are disappointed. The wordplay disappears in English 'idols' and 'images'.

Silver and gold were the costly materials of cult statues in Mesopotamia and Egypt, where a statue was ritually 'brought to life' by a mouth-opening ceremony; the psalm refuses this claim by calling it manufacture. Ibn Ezra notes that it is a disgrace that people worship their own creations. The KJV's 'men's hands' for 'adam is gendered: the Hebrew says 'humankind'.

philological_notes.note: 'their idols', formed from the root of 'etzev, 'pain': the writer may have meant the word to sound like 'their sorrows'. Not certain; the commentators say so.

verses.translation_literal: A mouth [belongs] to them, and they do not speak; eyes [belong] to them, and they do not see.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have a mouth, and it never speaks. They have eyes, and nothing ever looks back.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here begins the list of what is missing, and its form is the point: the Hebrew has no verb 'have', only 'a mouth to them', and then the blunt 'and not'. Each pair works as a small blow: 'a mouth to them / and not they speak'. Play it flat, as a litany, not as an outburst. The statue is made in the shape of a person, and the psalm lists each organ it was given and says what that organ fails to do.

Radak says the makers shaped them in human form but could not breathe a spirit into them. Meiri notes that these are only the shape of a mouth and the shape of an eye. Malbim sees an order: speech, sight, hearing, smell, touch, movement. The KJV 'They have mouths' makes it plural for pe, which is singular; the plural belongs to the English.

verses.translation_literal: Ears [belong] to them, and they do not hear; a nose [belongs] to them, and they do not smell.
verses.translation_dramatic: They have ears, worked into them with care, and no sound ever reaches them. They have a nose, and the smoke of the offering rises past it and is never breathed in.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm keeps its catalogue of senses going, and the rhythm matters: each line gives the idol a body part and takes its use away in the same breath, "X to them, and not...". Ibn Ezra notes that the list names four senses and leaves out eating, since an idol needs no such thing; the author is mocking an image that is fed daily with offerings it cannot touch. Here the two senses are the ones a worshipper depends on most: the god who hears the prayer and the god who smells the sacrifice. In the ancient Near East a deity was served with food, incense and fragrant smoke, and Israel's own texts speak of a "pleasing aroma" for the LORD. The jab is that the idol cannot even do what its priests claim it does.

The KJV ("noses have they, but they smell not") is accurate but flattens the Hebrew. The noun אַף is the ordinary word for nose, and also the word for anger, as in "his nose burned"; the audience hears at once that these gods cannot even flare in anger. The KJV also puts "noses" in the plural, while the Hebrew has the singular "a nose", a small oddity next to the dual "ears" (the dual form of a paired organ). Meiri and the Targum both read אַף as the organ of smell (the Targum has נְחִירֵי, "nostrils"). Read it aloud with a short pause after each "and not": it is a drumbeat of absence.

philological_notes.note: Nose, nostril; by extension anger, because the nose flares and snorts in rage. Here it is the organ only, but a Hebrew hearer would catch the second sense: the idol has no nose to burn.

Hiphil imperfect of the root for smell, with the longer ending -ûn that poetry sometimes keeps. In the Hiphil the verb can mean to smell, to take in a scent; it is the verb used elsewhere of God smelling a pleasing aroma.

verses.translation_literal: Their hands, and they do not feel; their feet, and they do not walk; they do not make a sound in their throat.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hands, and they cannot touch. Feet, and they cannot walk. Not a murmur, not even a whisper, rises in their throat.
verses.directors_commentary:
The litany ends with the limbs and the throat, and the grammar tightens: now there is not even 'to them', only 'their hands... and not they feel'. The line is a list of absences read at speed. 'Yemishun' means 'to feel by touch': Rashi ties it to Genesis 27:12, where Jacob fears his blind father will 'feel' him, and Metzudat Zion makes the same link.

The last line goes further than 'they do not speak' of v.5. The verb yehgu means a low sound, a murmur or coo: the same verb is used of a dove in Isaiah 38:14, as Meiri and Ibn Ezra point out. The statues cannot make even an animal's sound. The KJV's 'neither speak they through their throat' repeats v.5 and loses this step down from speech to mere sound; the ASV is the same; BBE's 'no sound comes from their throat' is closer.

philological_notes.note: 'they feel, grope': the sense of touch. Rashi links it to Isaac 'feeling' Jacob (Genesis 27:12).
'to murmur, to make a low sound'; used of a dove (Isaiah 38:14). The point: not even a sound without words.

verses.translation_literal: Like them will be those who make them, every one who [is] trusting in them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let those who made them become like them: every one of them who puts his trust in them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verdict follows the list, and the ancient commentators agree on its form: Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri say it is a prayer, 'may they become like them', not a plain statement. Metzudat David hears a curse on those who make gods of such things. The irony is exact: whoever makes a mouth that cannot speak and trusts it will end with a mouth that cannot speak, blind, deaf, and unable to move. People become what they worship.

KJV's 'are like unto them' and ASV's 'shall be like' turn the wish into a statement of fact or a prediction; the Hebrew is simply 'they will be', so the prayer sense is in the tone. The word 'trusting' is the first of the chapter's key verb, batach, which now turns round: v.9 will tell Israel whom to trust instead. The Hebrew 'like them' is the rare form kemohem, which sounds heavier than the ordinary kahem.

philological_notes.note: 'like them', a poetic form of the preposition; the commentators take what follows as a wish ('may they be').
'trusting, relying': the verb that the next three verses turn into a command to Israel.

verses.translation_literal: Israel, trust in YHWH! Their help and their shield [is] he.
verses.translation_dramatic: Israel, lean your weight on the LORD. He is their help. He is their shield.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the idol-makers' dead trust in verse 8, the psalm turns on a single word: 'betach', trust. The command is a singular imperative aimed at Israel as one body, and Radak says exactly this: 'he said betach to Israel as a whole' (Radak on 115:9). Verses 10 and 11 then switch to the plural 'bitchu' for the house of Aaron and for those who fear YHWH. So the KJV's 'trust thou' is a fair rendering of the singular; what the English cannot show is that the plural address returns two lines later. Let the first call be one voice speaking to a crowd, then split into groups.

The second half moves into the third person, 'their help and their shield', while the first half speaks to 'you'. This swerve is a known feature of the verse: Ibn Ezra compares the phrase to 'shield of your help' (Deut 33:29) and takes it to mean that YHWH has always been Israel's help and shield (Ibn Ezra on 115:9). It sounds like a leader calling, and the congregation answering. 'Magen' is a shield for a soldier to hold against arrows; Metzudat David glosses it as protection for the one who wears it (Metzudat David on 115:9). The BBE's 'breastplate' makes it armor for the chest; the Hebrew word is the shield. The idols have hands that cannot touch; here is a protector whose help is real.

philological_notes.note: Singular imperative, 'trust', addressed to Israel as one body. Verses 10-11 use the plural bitchu.
'And their shield'. A magen is the shield carried on the arm, not a breastplate as the BBE has it.

verses.translation_literal: House of Aaron, trust in YHWH! Their help and their shield [is] he.
verses.translation_dramatic: House of Aaron, you who serve at the altar: trust in the LORD. He is their help, and he is their shield.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain repeats exactly, and the only thing that changes is who is called. The house of Aaron are the priests; Ibn Ezra says that after naming Israel the psalm names God's holy ones, and Radak that the priests and Levites are the ones who stand before him continually, so their service should make them trust. Malbim reads the three groups as rising steps of trust and help.

A director should keep the refrain identical in each verse, so that the repetition builds like a litany and the audience hears who is next. The first line of each call is a short command; the second is the same line each time. The KJV 'he is their help' keeps the third person, as it should: the shift from the call to 'their' is the sound of the choir answering the leader. BBE's 'breastplate' for magen repeats its error from v.9.

verses.translation_literal: Fearers of YHWH, trust in YHWH! Their help and their shield [is] he.
verses.translation_dramatic: You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD. He is their help, and he is their shield.
verses.directors_commentary:
The third call is the open one. Who the 'fearers of YHWH' are was disputed among the old commentators. Rashi says they are the converts (gerim); Metzudat David and one view in Radak and Meiri say they are the pious among the nations; Radak's main view is that they are the wise who study in the house of the LORD. The phrase is not an ethnic term but a religious one, and a modern reader should hear it as the widest ring: Israel, then priests, then everyone who reveres God.

The KJV 'ye that fear the Lord' is accurate. The pair 'fear' and 'trust' is chosen: reverence and reliance go together. In the Hebrew the name YHWH is repeated twice in the line, and the repetition belongs to the refrain: the speaker is naming the one to whom they are all to turn.

philological_notes.note: 'those who fear YHWH': a group distinct from Israel and Aaron's house. Taken as converts, as pious gentiles, or as the devout inside Israel.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH has remembered us; he will bless, he will bless [obj] the house of Israel, he will bless [obj] the house of Aaron.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has remembered us. He will bless. He will bless the house of Israel. He will bless the house of Aaron.
verses.directors_commentary:
The congregation answers the call of verses 9-11. 'Has remembered us': in the Bible, God's remembering is not recall but action, the turning toward someone in a way that changes what happens. Radak reads it as the LORD who has remembered us always, in mercy (Radak on 115:12). Play the first 'he will bless' as a general promise with no object spoken, then the next two lines name the groups, Israel and Aaron, and verse 13 adds the third group, those who fear YHWH. The Hebrew builds by repetition, three beats of the same verb, like a drumbeat.

The KJV and ASV give 'he will bless us', and Webster sets 'us' in brackets. The Hebrew has no object after the first yevarekh at all; the English supplies one. It is better to leave it open, because the blessing is then about to fill itself in with names. Ibn Ezra also reports a view of R. Moshe, who read 'zekharanu' as 'our males' and 'the house of Israel' as the females. Ibn Ezra rejects it: the house of Aaron cannot be females, and the word comes from the root of remembering (Ibn Ezra on 115:12).

philological_notes.note: 'He has remembered us', perfect with the first-person plural suffix. Ibn Ezra takes it from zekhira (remembering) and not from zakhar 'male', against R. Moshe's reading, and notes the vowel under the resh does not fit 'male'.
Repeated three times. The first has no object and is general; the next two name Israel and then Aaron, and verse 13 adds those who fear YHWH.

verses.translation_literal: He will bless those who fear YHWH, the small with the great.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will bless those who fear the LORD: the small standing beside the great.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 13 extends the blessing of verse 12 to the third group called in verse 11, the fearers of YHWH, and adds a pairing: small with great. Say it as the last and widest circle. The sense of 'im', with, is the heart of it. The KJV's 'both small and great' turns the Hebrew's 'with' into a plain list; the Hebrew has them side by side. Ibn Ezra takes it to mean that the small are equal in the blessing with the great (Ibn Ezra on 115:13). Radak offers another sense: the small are blessed for the sake of the great (Radak on 115:13).

Radak also notes why the fearers are not called a 'house' as Israel and Aaron are: 'house' includes children, and children have no knowledge of what trust is (Radak on 115:13). In a world where status counted heavily, a promise that reaches the lowest rank and the highest in one breath is a leveling one. Let the line fall quietly and end the movement.

philological_notes.note: 'The small with the great'. 'Im' means together with, which the KJV's 'both ... and' flattens. Ibn Ezra: they are equal in the blessing; Radak: the small are blessed for the sake of the great.

verses.translation_literal: May YHWH add upon you, upon you and upon your sons.
verses.translation_dramatic: May the LORD add to you, add to you, to you and to your children after you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker turns from 'them' to 'you', and the voice becomes a priest's. The verb yosef is the short form, a wish: 'may he add'. The KJV 'shall increase you more and more' turns a prayer into a forecast and invents the 'more and more' to cover the doubled 'aleikhem', 'upon you, upon you'. The repetition is the point: the blessing is stacked on the same heads again and again, and then runs forward to the sons. Ibn Ezra notes that the verse spells out what the blessing is, an addition, as the curse is a lack. In an economy of fields, flocks and children, 'adding' is concrete: more grain, more animals, more heirs.

Say the doubled phrase twice, the second time lower, as though the speaker cannot stop adding.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil jussive of 'to add'. A wish or blessing formula, 'may he add'. Radak says it is spoken 'by way of prayer or prophecy'; Ibn Ezra says it spells out the blessing as an addition, the opposite of which is loss.
The doubled 'upon you' is deliberate emphasis and gives the verse its rhythm. The KJV hides it behind 'more and more'; YLT keeps it.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [are] you to YHWH, maker of heavens and earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed are you by the LORD, the maker of heaven and earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The wish becomes a declaration: 'blessed are you'. The lamed before YHWH marks the one from whom the blessing comes, which is why the KJV 'of the Lord' (old English for 'by') and the BBE 'the blessing of the Lord' both reach for the same sense. A modern reader hears 'of the Lord' as 'belonging to', which is not what is said. The title 'maker of heaven and earth' is the answer to the opening complaint of the psalm. The nations ask where Israel's God is; the idols are silver and gold, made by hands, while this God is the maker of the whole cosmos. Ibn Ezra reads it as authority over the upper and lower worlds, and Radak adds that he can bless whom he wills.

The participle 'oseh' is a present participle, 'making', not the KJV past 'which made'. Play the title as a standing fact: his hands are the ones that make.

philological_notes.note: The lamed marks agency, 'blessed by YHWH'. The KJV 'of the Lord' now reads as possession. The Targum renders it 'from before the LORD'.

A present participle in construct, 'maker of heavens and earth', a title of God rather than a report of a past act. Ibn Ezra links it to Genesis 2:4 ('in the day YHWH God made earth and heaven'), and says it means that God rules both the upper and lower realms.

verses.translation_literal: The heavens [are] heavens to YHWH, and the earth he has given to the sons of Adam.
verses.translation_dramatic: The heavens, the highest heavens, belong to the LORD. But the earth he has placed in the hands of humankind.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first clause repeats the noun: 'the heavens are heavens'. That is a Hebrew way of saying 'heavens in the full sense', the highest, his own. The KJV 'the heaven, even the heavens' keeps the repetition but turns the word into a singular and then a plural; the Hebrew has the same plural both times. The ASV 'heavens of Jehovah' is closer to the grammar. The second clause is the surprise: 'he has given', a perfect, a gift already made, and the 'sons of Adam' are the whole human family, not Israel alone.

The verse is read in two directions. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear a steward's office: humankind holds the earth as the LORD's appointed officials, and Radak says they can be removed from it. Meiri hears a choice: the earth is given so that people can freely decide how to use it. Both fit the polemic against the nations: the gods of the surrounding peoples are said to live in the heavens, but the heavens are the LORD's own, and the stewards of the earth are people, not idols.

Play the contrast: the first half is high and still, the second warmer, closer to the ground.

philological_notes.note: The noun is repeated, the first time with the article and the second without. It reads 'the heavens are heavens', an emphatic 'the very heavens'. Ibn Ezra, discussing the word, treats the plural form as 'two places'.
'He has given to the sons of Adam': a perfect verb, a gift already made. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as a trusteeship, with humans as officials of God over the earth.

verses.translation_literal: Not the dead will praise Yah, and not any going down [to] silence.
verses.translation_dramatic: The dead do not praise the LORD. Nor do any who go down into the silence.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood drops suddenly. After the earth given to the living, here are those who have left it. The Hebrew places 'not' first in each half, so the verse begins with a refusal twice: 'Not the dead … and not any …'. 'Yah' is the short form of the divine name, used in praise and in 'hallelu-yah' in the next verse. The KJV 'the Lord' erases the difference.

In the world of the psalm, praise is a thing done aloud, in the temple, with the body, and death ends it. Sheol is not a place of punishment here but of silence. The word 'dumah' means silence, and Ibn Ezra connects it to a root meaning 'cut off', while Radak and Metzudat Zion say it is the grave, a place of stillness. The KJV 'go down into silence' is good; the BBE 'the underworld' interprets. Later readers (Meiri, Metzudat David) take the verse to speak of the wicked, not of everyone who dies, which is a different reading than the plain sense; stage the plain one, a flat statement of what death does to praise.

Speak it quietly, without despair.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who go down to silence': a way of naming the dead, going down to the grave. Radak and Metzudat Zion take dumah as the grave, a place of silence; Ibn Ezra relates it to a root meaning to cut off, and says there is also another view that it comes from the word for silence.
The short form of the divine name, found in praise language. The KJV renders it 'the Lord', as it does YHWH.

verses.translation_literal: And we, we will bless Yah from now and until forever. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: But we, we will bless the LORD, from this hour and for all time. Praise the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn the previous verse prepared for. The Hebrew says 'and we' with the pronoun spelled out, 'va'anachnu', where the verb alone would have carried the subject: the stress is 'we, we are the ones who will bless'. The KJV 'But we' catches the contrast, though the Hebrew says 'and'. The speakers are the living, and the blessing they give returns, on a human scale, the blessing they were given in verses 12 to 15: the same verb, 'bless', now going upward. 'From now and until forever' is a stretch of time with no end; 'olam' covers the distant horizon, not an abstract eternity. Radak reads 'from now' as the present and 'until forever' as the world to come; Meiri and Metzudat David read it as life that does not end. The plain sense is simply that the praise will not stop.

The final 'hallelu-yah' is the closing cry of the psalm, a plural command to the congregation. Let the voice grow and then hold.

philological_notes.note: The independent pronoun with the verb adds emphasis: 'and we, we will bless'. It answers the 'he will bless' of verse 13 with the same root, so the blessing goes from God to people and back.
'From now and until forever'. Radak reads 'now' as the present time and 'olam' as the world to come.
A plural imperative, 'praise Yah': the call of the liturgy, and the final word of the psalm.
